cells.tense: You are here with it now, hands open, not deciding anything yet.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're tending and let it set its own pace for a week — feed it only when it visibly asks.
cells.core:
You're with what's growing and you haven't closed your hand around it. That's the whole trick, and most people lose it early. You can sit with something half-formed without naming it, without steering it, and the sitting is what lets it come up straight instead of bent toward you. Nothing you're doing is forcing a shape onto it, and that's why what comes out of your care looks like itself.

There's pull toward light in this — yours and the thing's. Watch a week go by and see what you actually fed. There's heat you have and aren't spending yet, and it's yours to spend how you choose. You can be the conditions something grows in. Most people only know how to be the hand that corrects it.
cells.sheetLine: You can stand in the middle of something unfinished and not close it.

cells.tense: You are already living in the version that hasn't arrived, steering by a future no one has written.
cells.ask: Name one thing you're keeping open and close it today — pick the real one out loud, even if it isn't the best of them.
cells.core:
You see what it could become and you can't put that down. Every stage of it gets imagined forward, revised, held up against the version that would be truer, and the imagining has become the care. You're not neglecting what's growing. You're hovering over it in a future tense with a hand on the lid. What's underneath stays a possibility and doesn't get the one thing it needs, which is to be allowed to be one actual thing with limits.

What's fixed doesn't shrink when you commit to it. Try picking one and letting it be that, today, with its flaws in the room. The shine you're after isn't earned by keeping everything open. It shows when something has grown the way it grew, not before.
cells.sheetLine: You're tending all the versions of it except the one that exists.

cells.tense: You are standing at a door you already walked through, still deciding whether to open it.
cells.ask: Put one small growing thing in front of you — a plant, a page, a person — and tend it badly for ten minutes without asking if you're doing it wrong.
cells.core:
There's ground in front of you and a hand that won't move toward it. Something back there made opening feel like the way things get taken, so you've kept it closed and called it being careful. You can grow things. What stopped is moving toward them. Whatever is coming up near you gets a patience that holds it off rather than a patience that lets it close.

You don't have to feel open to start. Tend one small thing without checking your own temperature first — and let what you see about the whole situation deepen as it goes. Not a verdict, just a look. Even ten minutes of contact changes what you can see about it later.

cells.tense: You are already shaping what comes next, and you're describing it as just how things went.
cells.ask: Catch one moment today where you steer something small — the actual moment — and say out loud that you chose it.
cells.core:
Things around you keep turning out a certain way, and you speak as if the turning did itself. But somebody decides what gets watered and what gets left. You do it in the small moves — which question gets asked, which effort gets made, which thing you let sit. You're not running the outcome; you're setting the conditions, and that's the work. It's already happening.

You don't need to see the whole road. One step of light is enough. Next time you're in the middle of a choice like that, name it to yourself: this was mine. That's all. You were already doing it; now it's something you can find again.

attempts.check: The record does not say the person in Too Little ever tried to nurture something and was hurt at it — I must locate them behind the present without saying what happened there. A reader could reasonably say they're not sealed at all, just tired, and that the door is the same. The ask still works if my read is wrong, because tending one square of ground produces the same evidence either way. The sentence that serves me more than them is the disowned-present line about the pen — it flatters the reader's ear and tells the person nothing they could disagree with.
